video.title: Why Was God Not in the FIRE? The Hebrew Words Behind 1 Kings 19
video.description:
Why was God not in the fire? In 1 Kings 19:11-12, Elijah stands on Mount Horeb while a great wind breaks the rocks, an earthquake shakes the mountain and a fire passes by, and three times the text says, "the LORD was not in" it. Then comes what the King James Version calls "a still small voice."

In this Bible study we read 1 Kings 19 through the Hebrew text. We follow Elijah from the fire on Carmel and Jezebel's threat to the juniper tree, where he prays, "It is enough." We see how the writer places him where Moses stood: forty days and forty nights, Horeb the mount of God, "the cave," and the LORD who "passed by" (Exodus 33:22; 34:6). We look at the three signs of Sinai, wind (ruach), earthquake (ra'ash) and fire (esh), and at the three Hebrew words of verse 12, qol demamah daqqah. Qol can mean voice or sound. Demamah comes from a root meaning to be still, to fall silent, and its only other uses are Job 4:16 and Psalm 107:29, where God "maketh the storm a calm." Daqqah means thin or fine, the word used for the thin ears in Pharaoh's dream, the manna and the incense beaten small. We compare the Septuagint, the Geneva Bible, the King James and modern translations, and see why some render the phrase "a sound of sheer silence."

Then we look at what Elijah did when he heard it, the same question and the same answer in verses 9-10 and 13-14, and God's three gifts: a task, a successor in Elisha, and the 7,000 who had not bowed to Baal. Finally we follow the thread to Mark 4:39, the Transfiguration in Matthew 17, and Psalm 46:10.

All Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.

Has there been a time when God felt silent to you, and you later saw He had been there all along? Share it in the comments, and subscribe for more studies beneath the verse.

transcript.text: A man sits deep inside a cave on the mountain of God.
He's walked 40 days and 40 nights to get here.
Outside, a wind tears the mountain apart and breaks the rocks in pieces.
Then the ground shakes.
Then fire.
Here's the question almost nobody asks.
When all of that was over, what did Elijah actually hear?
Most of us were taught the answer in four words.
A still, small voice.
We picture God speaking softly, almost in a whisper, a gentle voice inside the heart.
Generations of sermons, books, and prayers have been built on that picture.
But the Hebrew text does not say voice in the way we think.
The three words are qol demahha dahhka.
The first word can mean voice, but it just as often means sound.
The second word means silence or stillness.
The third means thin, fine, crushed small.
Put them side by side and you get something closer to a sound of thin silence.
Several modern translations now render it almost exactly that way.
So the first answer is this, what came after the fire may not have been a quiet voice at all.
It may have been a silence so complete that Elijah could hear it.
And that changes far more than a phrase.
It changes why God met this particular man in this particular way, on this particular mountain.
Let us start where the text starts.
First Kings chapter 19 does not begin in a cave.
It begins with a threat.
In chapter 18, Elijah has just stood on Mount Carmel against 450 prophets of Baal.
He has prayed, and fire has fallen from heaven.
First Kings chapter 18, verse 38 says, Then the fire of the Lord fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.
Then, a few verses later, the long drought breaks in what the text calls the third year.
Verse 45 says the heaven was black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain.
Hold on to those two things: fire and wind.
We will meet them again.
It should have been the greatest day of Elijah's life.
And then one message arrives from Queen Jezebel.
First Kings chapter 19, verse 2.
Then Jezebel sent a messenger unto Elijah saying, So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I make not thy life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time.
Verse 3 says, And when he saw that, he arose, and went for his life.
The man who called down fire runs.
He runs south out of the northern kingdom, through Judah, all the way to Beersheba at the edge of the desert.
He leaves his servant there, and then he keeps going alone.
Verse 4.
But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree.
And he requested for himself that he might die, and said, It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.

transcript.text: So already before we reach the second word, voice is only one possible reading.
The second word is the heart of it, demamah.
It comes from a root, damaham, which means to be silent, to be still, to stop.
Let me show you where that root appears because this is where the translation flattens what the Hebrew is doing.
In Joshua chapter 10 verse 12, Joshua says, Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon.
The word for stand still is dohm from this root.
The sun does not whisper, it stops.
In Leviticus chapter 10 verse 3, after Aaron's two sons die before the Lord, the text says, and Aaron held his peace.
The Hebrew is vayiddom.
Aaron fell silent.
There are no words in grief like that.
In Psalm 4 verse 4, the King James says, commune with your own heart upon your bed and be still.
Be still is the same root.
In Psalm 37 verse 7, rest in the Lord and wait patiently for him.
The Hebrew for rest there is dohm.
Be silent before the Lord.
And in Psalm 62 verse 1, truly my soul waiteth upon God.
The word behind waiteth is a close relative, dumiyyah, silence.
A more literal rendering would be, my soul is silence toward God.
Every one of those uses is about stillness, stopping, or silence.
None of them is about speaking softly.
Now the noun itself, demamah, is rare.
As far as the concordances show, it appears only three times in the whole Hebrew Bible.
Once here and twice more.
Each of the other two uses helps us read this one.
The first is in Job chapter 4 verse 16.
Eliphaz is describing a terrifying night vision.
Verse 15 says, a spirit passed before his face and the hair of his flesh stood up.
Then verse 16, it stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof.
An image was before mine eyes.
There was silence, and I heard a voice saying, there was silence.
That is demamah.
In fact, the Hebrew can be read very literally as, silence, and a voice I heard.
Some read that as silence first, and then a voice.
Others read it as one thing, a silent voice, a whisper.
The second is in Psalm 107 verse 29.
This is a psalm about sailors caught in a storm at sea.
They cry out to the Lord, and verse 29 says, He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still.
The word translated calm is demamah.
God takes a storm and turns it into stillness.
Think about that for a moment.
The only other place this noun is used of a storm, it describes the moment after the storm stops.
That is exactly where we find it in 1 Kings.
After wind, after earthquake, after fire, stillness.
Now the third word, dakah.
It comes from a root, daqaq, which means to crush, to grind fine, to beat into powder.
The adjective form means thin, fine, small.
In Genesis chapter 41, Pharaoh dreams of seven lean cows and seven thin ears of grain.
The thin ears in verse 6 are described with this word.

transcript.text: And he says exactly the same thing.
Most of us pass over that.
But it tells us something very gentle about how God works.
The silence did not instantly fix Elijah.
It did not erase his fear in one moment.
It did not make him say the right words.
He was still tired.
He still felt alone.
And God does not scold him for it.
Instead, God gives him three things.
The first is a task.
Go, return on thy way to the wilderness of Damascus.
He is to anoint Hazael as king over Syria, Jehu as king over Israel, and Elisha as prophet in his place.
Elijah thought the story was over.
God tells him the story is still being written and he still has a part in it.
The second is a successor.
Elisha.
Elijah will not carry this alone forever.
Someone will take up the mantle.
The third is the correction of his loneliness.
Verse 18.
Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal.
Twice, God answers.
Elijah could not see them.
They were not on Carmel shouting.
They were not in the headlines of that age.
They were quiet.
Faithful people scattered through the land who simply had not bowed.
Do you notice the pattern?
The fire and the wind were loud and God was not in them.
The silence was thin, and it sent Elijah out of the cave.
And the faithful remnant was hidden, quiet, unseen.
And yet it was there all along.
The whole chapter is teaching the same thing in three different ways.
God is often at work where it is quietest.
There is one more thread, and it reaches far beyond Elijah's lifetime.
Remember Psalm 107 verse 29.
He maketh the storm a calm so that the waves thereof are still.
That stillness was de mama.
Centuries later, on the Sea of Galilee, a storm breaks over a small fishing boat.
The disciples wake Jesus in terror.
And Mark chapter 4 verse 39 says, And he arose and rebuked the wind and said unto the sea, Peace, be still.
And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
The gospel is written in Greek, not Hebrew, so this is not the same word.
But many readers have heard the psalm behind the scene.
The disciples' response in verse 41

transcript.text: Verse three says, and behold, there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him.
Elias is the Greek form of Elijah.
Think about who is standing there, the two great prophets whose stories meet at Horeb.
Jewish tradition even remembered the cleft and the cave as one place.
Moses, who saw God pass by and heard his name proclaimed.
Elijah, who heard the thin silence and covered his face.
And now they stand on a mountain beside Jesus.
Then a bright cloud overshadows them and verse five says,
Behold a voice out of the cloud which said, this is my beloved son in whom I am well pleased.
Hear ye him.
Hear ye him, listen to him.
I would not build a doctrine on that connection.
The text does not draw the line for us.
But it is hard to read it without remembering a man who once stood on a mountain and was taught to listen in a new way.
Before we bring this home, there is one verse we should handle carefully because people often connect it with this passage.
Psalm 46:10.
Be still and know that I am God.
It is a beautiful verse and it is often quoted together with the still small voice.
But the Hebrew word there is different.
It is harpu from a root that means to let go, to relax your grip, to stop striving.
It is a command spoken into the noise of war where verse nine says, God makes wars to cease.
So the two passages are not the same word, but they do share a pattern.
In both, God is known not by adding more force, but by bringing the force to an end.
Let us pull this together.
Elijah came to Horeb exhausted, frightened and convinced he was alone.
He had seen God answer by fire and perhaps he expected God to meet him the same way again.
God showed him wind that split the mountain, an earthquake and fire, the very signs of Sinai and of Carmel.
And three times the text says, the Lord was not in them.
Then came three Hebrew words, a sound, a silence, thin as frost and fine as incense.
That noun appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible and each time it sits close to stillness and hush.
When Elijah heard it, he covered his face and stepped out to meet God.
